documentation.range: The species occurs at elevations between sea level and 200 m asl. Based on historical records, it is known from the Pampean region of Argentina (Buenos Aires, Córdoba, La Pampa, and Santa Fe provinces), Uruguay (a few localities in Rocha, San José, and Montevideo departments), and the state of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil. However, it has not been registered in Uruguay since 1982, and the last record from Brazil dates back to 1992 (Deutsch et al. 2024). The latest national assessments have assigned it the status of Vulnerable in Argentina (Vaira et al. 2012) and Uruguay (Maneyro and Carreira 2015), and Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) in Brazil (Ministry of Environment 2022). A major search effort in the three countries, involving passive acoustic monitoring and citizen science tools, failed to recover recent records of this species in Brazil and Uruguay (Deutsch et al. 2024). This supports the notion that the species is Possibly Extinct in both countries. Thus, the remnant subpopulations of the species would be exclusively located in the Pampean region of Argentina (Deutsch et al. 2017, Deutsch et al. 2024). While the estimated distribution area for Argentina currently includes both the Pampean and Espinal regions, recent studies using potential distribution models predict low habitat suitability in the Espinal and marginal areas of the Pampean region (Deutsch et al. 2024). Considering the records obtained from several data sources (herpetological collections, field monitoring and citizen science) ranging from 1879 to 2023 (Deutsch et al. 2024) plus new records from 2024, the historical extent of occurrence (EOO) is 508,805 km2 and the historical area of occurrence (AOO) is 1,812 km2. However, when estimations are calculated based only on records obtained in the past 15 years, the current EOO is reduced to 322,283 km2, approximately 37% of the historical distribution, and the current AOO is reduced to 972 km2.
documentation.population:
There have been no records of the species in Uruguay since 1982 (Deutsch et al. 2024). It might be considered extinct in Uruguay, as some exhaustive sampling efforts carried out in historical sites (Laguna de Castillos and Valizas in Rocha, Delta del Tigre in San Jose, and Montevideo) have not detected the presence of the species (Gambarotta et al. 1999, Bardier and Maneyro 2015, Deutsch et al. 2024). Additionally, the species was not found during surveys in water bodies like those used by this species to breed in Cerro Verde Protected Area (Uruguay) and surrounding areas during 2007–2009 (Bardier and Maneyro 2015), and in Boca de Cufré, Arazati, Arroyo Maldonado, Laguna El Diario, Cerro Verde y Cabo Polonio during 2019–2020 (Deutsch et al. 2024) despite historical records showing the species presence in the area.

For many years, the last documented records for Brazil were from 1980 (Braun and Braun 1980). Recent research applying citizen science techniques was able to obtain two more recent records dating from 1991 and 1992 (Deutsch et al. 2024). The species was once commonly found, even outside of the reproductive season, and was one of the few amphibian species familiar to local residents within its range. Search efforts using different sampling techniques have been carried out by several researchers, especially at the Estação Ecológica do Taim and Santa Vitória do Palmar, without the species being recorded. Since 2007, different researchers have carried out ecological studies in the region by sampling and monitoring the environmental impact of the installation of wind turbine projects. More recent research, applying citizen science and automatic recorders, also failed to obtain current records of the species in Brazil. Both researchers and local residents say that the species is no longer seen (D. Loebmann, M. Freire, I. Machado, P. Colombo, and L.F.M. Fonte pers. comm. 2024). There is limited remaining natural habitat; it has been converted into rice plantations, urban areas, and wind farms.

The species is still known to exist in Argentina, however, it is considered to be rare (Vaira et al. 2012). The population is thought to be in significant decline, but probably at a rate of less than 30% over the past fifteen years. Specifically, in some areas of the Pampas region the species appears to have declined (G. Agostini pers. comm. 2017). Results of 12 years of sampling indicate that although the area of distribution of the species is extensive within the Pampean Region, the population status is not uniform (G. Agostini pers. comm. 2017). The species has disappeared from several localities belonging to the Pampa Ondulada and the Pampa Floodplain (north-east and central-east of the Province of Buenos Aires, respectively). Data available from herpetological collections show relatively frequent historical occurrence in areas where the species has since disappeared in association with the replacement of natural habitat due to urbanization (e.g., La Plata, Tigre and Escobar). Additionally, records in rural landscapes for both sub-regions are increasingly scarce (G. Agostini pers. comm. 2017). The last record of the species in the Pampa Mesopotámica sub-region (Province of Entre Ríos) dates back to 1995 and five years of field work have been unable to confirm its presence at historic sites (G. Agostini pers. comm. 2017).

New information indicates that the species occurs more frequently in two specific areas in Argentina (Agostini et al. 2016, Deutsch et al. 2017). One area is located in the northwest (Pampa Interior) and the other in the eastern dunes barrier of the Atlantic Coast of Buenos Aires. Both areas are separated by c. 590 km but share some similar characteristics in soil composition associated with low productivity, psammophile grasslands which have experienced fewer impacts from agricultural activities than other sub regions where the species occurs (Soriano et al. 1991). Therefore, the higher frequency of occurrence of the species could be related to a habitat preference for pastures with sandy soils, as indicated for the subpopulations of Uruguay (Maneyro and Carreira 2012, Maneyro et al. 2019), or might indicate that these subpopulations are relictual and remain only in areas that have been less impacted by anthropogenic activities (G. Agostini pers. comm. 2017). With all of this taken in account, it is considered to be severely fragmented because more than 50% of the global population exist in habitat patches that are smaller than would be required to support a viable population, and separated from other habitat patches by a large distance which mature individuals cannot disperse.

A major search effort in the three countries, involving passive acoustic monitoring and citizen science tools, failed to recover recent records of this species in Brazil and Uruguay (Deutsch et al. 2024).
documentation.habitats: This frog occurs in temperate grasslands and shrublands, on the ground near temporary waterbodies and in open areas (Basso 1990). It has low reproductive potential with a brief reproductive period after heavy rainfalls (Basso 1990, Vaira et al. 2012, Agostini and Deutsch pers. comm. 2024). The eggs are laid on the bottom of temporary ponds. It can be found in roadside ditches and in irrigated cropland (G. Agostini pers. comm. 2024). However, it is thought that the species uses these types of artificial wetlands because natural or pristine environments are almost non-existent (Perrone et al. 2022). In areas where extensive crops (monocultures) are predominant, the occurrence of the species is rare (Agostini et al. 2021, Deutsch et al. 2024).
documentation.threats:
Habitat loss from agricultural and residential development poses a major threat, as does water and soil pollution resulting from agriculture, industry, and human settlements. Areas in Argentina with monocultures coincide with more than 70% of the species' distribution (Vaira et al. 2012). Research by Costa et al. (2018) shows the negative effects of the cholinesterase-inhibiting insecticide chlorpyrifos (CPF) on the defence mechanism sounds emitted by tadpoles of this species.

At present, both areas where the species is known to occur in Argentina are subject to accelerated habitat modification (Deutsch et al. 2024). In the Inland Pampa sub-region, the expansion of the agricultural frontier towards traditionally low-burden and livestock-bearing soils is ongoing (Agostini et al. 2016, 2020, Perrone et al. 2022), while urban development is the main threat facing coastal environments in Buenos Aires (Ibáñez 2023, Agostini and Bilenca 2024). In general, the species has disappeared from urbanized environments and the current records from the Atlantic coast of Buenos Aires are from areas where urbanization is relatively recent. Therefore, it is expected that, as in other localities, the species will decline as the impacts of agriculture and urbanization intensify (G. Agostini pers. comm. 2024). 

In Uruguay, its historical localities are closely associated with areas of urban growth for tourism purposes, especially the eastern locations of the country (Maneyro et al. 2019). The town near the border between the departments of San José and Montevideo (Delta del Tigre) is also threatened by urban growth, including the construction of roads and the presence of chemical industries (Langone 2017), and forest plantations (Deutsch et al. 2024). In Brazil, the loss and fragmentation of suitable habitat for the species appears to be primarily associated with the expansion of rice cultivation and forest plantations (Deutsch et al. 2024).

In addition, the species is subject to persecution because of unfounded beliefs that it is venomous. It is also collected illegally for the pet trade and for scientific research (Deutsch et al. 2021).

Climate change, which generates variations in rainfall regimes and extended droughts, has had an impact on the reproductive success of the species. This problem is exacerbated by human activities that modify the structure of the wetlands. A recent study showed that larvae of this species are unable to metamorphose as ponds are drained and dry out before individuals complete the larval cycle (Deutsch et al. in prep).
documentation.measures:
Conservation Actions In-Place
There are records of the presence of the species in several protected areas. However, in Argentina, most of them are historical records (Reserva Natural El Destino, Parque Nacional Ciervo de los Pantanos) and the recent ones belong to areas protected by law but without effective protection (Refugio de Vida Silvestre-Reserva Natural Integral Bahía de Samborombón, Reserva Natural Punta Lara). In Uruguay, its historical records are within or close to the following conservation units: Parque Nacional Cabo Polonio, Área de Manejo de Hábitats and/or Especies Cerro Verde e Islas de la Coronilla and the Área Protegida con Recursos Manejados Humedales del Santa Lucía (Maneyro et al. 2019). In Brazil, there are historical records for Estação Ecológica do Taim.

Each country (Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay) has completed the Amphibian Conservation Needs Assessment (see www.amphibianark.org) for this species (Zank et al. 2020, Agostini and Deutsch 2021, Carreira et al. 2022).

A tri-national research and conservation endeavour known as the "Giant of the Pampas" is currently underway (https://gigantedospampas.wixsite.com/english), encompassing collaboration among researchers and conservationists from Argentina, Brazil, and Uruguay. This initiative aims to ascertain the population status of this species by amalgamating various data sources, including herpetological collections, citizen science initiatives, and fieldwork, as well as employing diverse monitoring techniques (Maneyro et al. 2019).

In Uruguay, the species is protected through national legislation by Ley de Fauna (Nº 9481 y decretos reglamentarios). It has been identified as a priority species in the Sistema Nacional de Áreas Protegidas, and it is listed as Vulnerable VU B1ab(iii) in the National Red List (Maneyro et al. 2019). Finally, mitigation of the effects of the advancing urban frontier in coastal areas where this species occurs is recommended (Maneyro et al. 2019).

In Brazil, progress has been made in establishing working agreements within the Giant of the Pampas project, including several institutions such as the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul, the National Center for Reptile and Amphibian Research and Conservation of the Chico Mendes Institute for Biodiversity Conservation of the Brazilian Ministry of the Environment, and the Curicaca Institute to further delineate research into the causes of the decline of this species in Brazil.

In Argentina, a citizen science programme has been ongoing since 2015 monitoring the occurrence of the species in real time (Deutsch et al. 2017). This programme has successfully gathered, to date, over 1,100 confirmed records. Additionally, in 2021, it initiated a Rescue and Relocation Plan, which involves engaging local communities coexisting with the species to report encounters with individuals in risky situations (e.g. on busy streets, in backyard settings). Upon receiving a rescue call, members of the team or participating partners capture the animal and release it in a pre-selected area known to be suitable for the species. Additionally, two working agreements were signed with two municipalities located in one of the areas identified as priorities for the species (General Lavalle and La Costa). Each year, educational and awareness workshops on the species' conservation are coordinated with the education secretariats in both localities. Also, in 2021, the municipality of General Lavalle declared this species of local interest.

Conservation Needed
Remnants of natural grasslands and associated wetlands must receive conservation priority, and increasing coverage of protected areas (private and public) could offer an opportunity to conserve grassland patches. This is particularly suitable for the Flooding Pampas in Argentina, where other conservation strategies that recognize and encourage alternative economic uses like sustainable cattle-raising (e.g. Alianza de Pastizal, Altmann and Berger Filho 2020, Vaccaro et al. 2020) have been extensively working in the same direction. In addition, better policy legislation to control human activities advancing on the remnants of native grassland and associated wetlands is required. Listing the species under CITES, along with increased monitoring on Argentina's border areas to prevent the export of specimens, is recommended to address the threat of illegal international trade of the species.

Research Needed
More information is needed on this species' distribution, population status, threats, and harvest trends. Monitoring international demand and trade of this species is also recommended (Maneyro et al. 2019). Population genetics studies are needed to evaluate future in situ and population management.
documentation.use_trade: In the Pampean Region of Argentina, it is collected for the domestic market and for scientific purposes at the national level (Deutsch et al. 2020). There is some data about the species being illegally exported from Argentina to Uruguay (Deutsch et al. 2020). The 2004 assessment suggested that this species was collected for the international pet trade, eggs were sold internationally for scientific research, and captive breeding probably occurred at high levels. However, there is no official data from the international legal market that confirms this suggestion (Deutsch et al. 2020).
documentation.rationale: Listed as Vulnerable because the species has an AOO of 972 km<sup>2</sup> with a continuous decline observed in EOO, AOO and habitat quality due to intense agricultural and urban development pressures. The population is considered to be severely fragmented, and there are declines in the population due to habitat loss and intense persecution.
documentation.taxonomic_notes:
Specimens from Mendoza, Argentina, previously assigned to this species, actually belong to Ceratophrys cranwelli (G. Agostini pers. comm. 2024). Finally, despite extensive survey efforts in Entre Rios (Argentina) as part of recent studies aimed at defining the current distribution of the species (Deutsch et al. 2024), the only records for this province consist of nine specimens collected in the Paraná locality, initially assigned as Trigonophrys rugiceps but later synonymized with C. ornata. The specific assignment of these individuals is incorrect, likely corresponding to C. cranwelli (Agostini and Deutsch pers. comm. 2024).

Brusquetti and Lavilla (2006) suggested that reports of this species for Paraguay are based on specimens of Ceratophrys cranwelli. The historical record of “Montevideo, Uruguay” based on a specimen deposited in the Royal Museum of Natural History of Belgium (Museu Royal d 'Histoire Naturelle, Brussels) (Cochran 1955) requires confirmation (Maneyro et al. 2019).
